Vignette: Amara

Amara is a 74-year-old woman who has spent the better part of her life working the land. She rises before dawn most mornings, her hands already knowing what her mind has not yet caught up to - which rows need tending, which soil needs turning. Agriculture is not simply her occupation; it is the rhythm by which she has always measured time, seasons, and her own worth. She is partnered, has been for decades, and her companion of many years shares the small home they keep near the fields where she works.

Approximately three years ago, Amara was raped by a man she knew - a supervisor on the agricultural cooperative where she labored. It happened at the end of a long workday, in a storage shed at the far edge of the property, when most of the other workers had already gone home. She did not scream. She tells herself now, quietly and with a shame that sits like a stone in her chest, that she did not scream because she was afraid no one would come. She walked home afterward in the fading light, washed herself, and said nothing to her partner that evening. She said nothing for a very long time.

In the weeks that followed, Amara returned to work because she had no choice - the family depended on her income. She avoided the storage shed, taking longer routes across the fields, sometimes arriving late to tasks that required her to pass near that part of the property. Her coworkers noticed she had become quieter, but attributed it to age, to tiredness. She let them believe that. At home, she stopped sleeping through the night. She would wake at two or three in the morning, her heart pounding as though she had been running, the darkness of the bedroom pressing down on her in a way it never had before. She began leaving a lamp on.

The smell of certain fertilizers - one in particular that had been stored in that shed - now sends her back there instantly. She does not choose to go. Her body simply arrives: the weight of him, the sound of the corrugated roof shaking in the wind, the particular quality of the late afternoon light through a gap in the wall. She has learned to step away from these moments quickly, to press her thumbnail into her palm, to focus on the texture of the soil beneath her feet. But some days it is not enough, and she simply sits down in the middle of a row and waits for herself to return.

She has told her partner only fragments of what happened - enough that he knows something was done to her, not enough that she has had to watch his face fully absorb it. She fears his anger, and she fears, more quietly, his pity. She has carried the fuller weight of it largely alone, and that aloneness has hollowed something out in her. She no longer takes pleasure in the small things that used to sustain her - the particular green of new seedlings, the company of the women she works alongside, the evening meal shared with her partner. She participates in these things, but from a slight distance, as though watching herself do them from just behind her own shoulder.

She is easily startled now. A door slamming, a man's raised voice somewhere across the field - her body responds before her mind can intervene. She has become watchful in a way that exhausts her, scanning faces, tracking exits, noting who is nearby when she is working in an isolated area. She is rarely alone on the land anymore, which is a loss of its own kind, because solitude in the fields was once where she felt most herself.

Amara does not use the word trauma when she speaks about what happened to her. She says, simply, that something was taken from her. She is not wrong.
